abstract.p: Tumorigenesis and progression are driven by dysregulated genes and signaling pathways, with cellular metabolic reprogramming being a hallmark that supports neoplastic growth. Alanyl-tRNA Synthetase 1 (AARS1), a key enzyme with dual roles in metabolism and gene expression regulation, has emerged as a critical focus in cancer and disease research. As a member of the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (AARS) family, AARS1 canonically catalyzes the attachment of alanine to its cognate transfer RNA (tRNA) to ensure fidelity in protein synthesis. Emerging evidence reveals non-canonical roles of AARS1 in tumor biology, including regulation of metabolic reprogramming, cell proliferation, apoptosis, and intracellular signal sensing—all of which directly impact tumor growth and patient prognosis. Beyond cancer, dysregulated AARS1 (via abnormal expression or pathogenic mutations) is linked to a spectrum of non-malignant disorders, including Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease (a hereditary peripheral neuropathy), adult-onset leukoencephalopathy, recurrent acute liver failure, and sulfide dysplasia. These associations arise from disrupted cellular homeostasis and impaired physiological functions caused by AARS1-mediated pathway dysregulation. Notably, AARS1’s ability to sense lactate and catalyze lysine lactylation—a newly identified post-translational modification (PTM)—represents a novel mechanism linking metabolic dysregulation to disease pathogenesis. Dysregulated AARS1 contributes to tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and treatment resistance, while its mutations drive the onset of several neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders. Unraveling the molecular mechanisms of AARS1, particularly its lactylation-related functions, will deepen our understanding of cellular metabolism in disease and identify novel therapeutic targets for precise diagnosis and treatment of tumors and other disorders. Furthermore, AARS1 holds significant promise as a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target, offering new avenues for precision medicine in both oncology and non-malignant conditions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (AARSs) are a family of evolutionarily conserved enzymes that serve as the “molecular link” between genetic code and protein synthesis. By catalyzing the covalent attachment of specific amino acids to their corresponding transfer RNAs (tRNAs), AARSs ensure the accurate translation of mRNA into functional proteins—an essential process for maintaining cellular homeostasis across all living organisms [1]. Over the past three decades, research has expanded beyond the canonical translational roles of AARSs, uncovering their non-canonical functions in cell signaling, metabolism, and stress response—many of which are dysregulated in disease [2, 3].

Alanyl-tRNA Synthetase 1 (AARS1), a member of the AARS family, has gained increasing attention due to its unique dual roles in protein synthesis and disease pathogenesis. In tumor cells, AARS1 exhibits two pivotal non-canonical functions: acting as an intracellular lactate sensor and catalyzing lysine lactylation—a Post-Translational Modification (PTM) first identified in 2019 that regulates metabolism, gene expression, and cell fate in cancer [4, 5]. This lactylation-mediated mechanism provides a direct link between the Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis in tumors) and malignant progression, offering a new lens to understand metabolic reprogramming in cancer [5, 6].

Beyond oncology, AARS1 is implicated in multiple non-malignant disorders. Pathogenic mutations in the AARS1 gene are a well-established cause of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 N (CMT2N), an inherited peripheral neuropathy characterized by progressive motor and sensory dysfunction [7–9]. Additionally, AARS1 mutations have been linked to adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP), recurrent acute liver failure, and sulfide dysplasia—highlighting its pleiotropic roles in maintaining nervous system and metabolic homeostasis [10–13].

Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in our understanding of AARS1, particularly concerning the precise atomic details of its lactate-sensing ability, the complete repertoire of its lactylation substrates beyond well-studied transcription factors, and the nuanced tissue-specific mechanisms by which AARS1 mutations drive diverse non-cancer diseases. This review comprehensively summarizes the molecular biology of AARS1, its lactylation-mediated functions in tumors, and its role in non-malignant disorders. By integrating recent structural, biochemical, and clinical evidence, we aim to highlight AARS1 as a potential therapeutic target and diagnostic biomarker, while critically assessing current knowledge, identifying existing limitations, and outlining future directions to address these unresolved questions in the field.

sec.title: Structural and functional basis of AARS1
Structural features: conservation and domain specialization
sec.p: AARS1 is highly evolutionarily conserved, with >60% amino acid sequence identity between Escherichia coli and human orthologs—reflecting its essential role in protein synthesis ADDIN EN.CITE (3, 14). In humans, the AARS1 gene is localized to chromosome 16q22.1 and encodes a 968-amino acid polypeptide with three functionally distinct domains (Figure 1), each critical to its canonical and non-canonical functions:

caption.p: Schematic of the human AARS1 protein structure. The three functional domains (aminoacylation, editing, and C-terminal) are shown with key residues/motifs and their associated functions. Functional domains of AlaRS including catalytic domain (in blue) with key residue R329 (associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 N, CMT2N), tRNA binding domain (in green), editing domain (in pink) with key residue T606 (associated with infantile-onset Alpers-like spinal muscular atrophy, ALSP), and C-Ala domain (in orange) with key residue E788 (associated with CMT2N)

sec.title: Aminoacylation domain (residues 1–455)
sec.p: This N-terminal domain is the catalytic core of AARS1, responsible for recognizing alanine and its cognate tRNA (tRNA^Ala). It contains a conserved ATP-binding pocket and a tRNA^Ala recognition motif that ensures specific aminoacylation—key to preventing translational errors [3, 14]. Pathogenic mutations in this domain (e.g., N71Y, G102R) disrupt catalytic activity, though some mutations (e.g., R329H) spare aminoacylation while driving CMT2N via alternative mechanisms [9, 15].

sec.title: Editing domain (residues 456–757)
sec.p: Also known as the “proofreading domain,” this central region hydrolyzes misactivated amino acids (e.g., serine, glycine) or mismatched aminoacyl-tRNAs (e.g., Ser-tRNA^Ala) to maintain translational fidelity [16, 17]. Loss-of-editing activity (e.g., due to the E688G mutation) leads to protein misfolding and neurodegeneration, as observed in ALSP [12]. Notably, this domain also contains a lactate-binding site that mediates AARS1’s non-canonical role as a lactate sensor [5].

sec.title: C-terminal domain (residues 758–968)
sec.p: This domain, also called the oligomerization domain, facilitates AARS1 dimerization and contains a conserved nuclear localization signal (NLS). In normal cells, AARS1 is predominantly cytoplasmic; however, in tumors, the NLS mediates nuclear translocation—enabling AARS1 to regulate transcription and DNA damage repair [5, 18]. Mutations in this domain (e.g., E788A, D893N) disrupt AARS1’s subcellular localization and interaction with neuropilin 1 (NRP1), a key driver of CMT2N [9].

sec.title: Canonical function: ensuring translational fidelity in protein synthesis
sec.p: Under physiological conditions, AARS1’s primary role is to mediate alanine incorporation into nascent proteins via a two-step ATP-dependent reaction (Fig. 2):

sec.title: Amino acid activation
sec.p: AARS1 binds alanine and ATP, catalyzing the formation of an alanyl-AMP intermediate (with release of pyrophosphate, PPi). This step is driven by ATP hydrolysis and is highly specific—ensuring only alanine is activated [3, 14].

sec.title: tRNA charging
sec.p: The alanyl moiety from alanyl-AMP is transferred to the 3’-hydroxyl group of tRNA^Ala, generating alanyl-tRNA (Ala-tRNA^Ala) and releasing AMP. Ala-tRNA^Ala then delivers alanine to the ribosome for translation [16, 17].

Dysregulation of this process (e.g., via mutations or reduced expression) leads to translational errors, such as misincorporation of serine or glycine into proteins. These errors cause protein misfolding, ER stress, and cellular dysfunction—underlying neurodegenerative diseases like CMT2N and ALSP [12, 17]. For example, the T606I mutation in the editing domain impairs proofreading, leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins and white matter lesions in ALSP patients [12].

caption.p: The two-step canonical reaction catalyzed by AARS1. Step 1: Alanine and ATP are converted to alanyl-AMP (intermediate) and PPi. Step 2: Alanyl-AMP transfers alanine to tRNA^Ala, forming Ala-tRNA^Ala (the active form for translation) and releasing AMP

sec.title: Aberrant AARS1 expression, localization, and lactylation in tumors
Aberrant AARS1 expression: a marker of malignant progression
sec.p: Across multiple tumor types, AARS1 is consistently upregulated at both the mRNA and protein levels—correlating with advanced disease and poor prognosis (Table 1). This overexpression is driven by oncogenic signaling pathways (e.g., MYC, PI3K/AKT) that promote metabolic reprogramming and protein synthesis in tumors [5, 18].

sec.p: In breast cancer, for example, AARS1 overexpression is observed in 72% of invasive ductal carcinomas, and patients with high AARS1 levels have a 3.2-fold higher risk of distant metastasis compared to those with low expression [5]. In leukemia, AARS1 upregulation promotes drug resistance by enhancing lactate metabolism and DNA damage repair—enabling tumor cells to survive genotoxic stress [6].

sec.title: Nuclear translocation of AARS1: a switch to oncogenic functions
sec.p: In normal cells, AARS1 is primarily cytoplasmic (where it mediates translation). In tumors, however, AARS1 undergoes partial nuclear translocation—driven by activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, which phosphorylates AARS1’s C-terminal domain and enhances NLS activity [5, 18]. Nuclear AARS1 exerts two key oncogenic functions:

sec.title: Transcriptional regulation
sec.p: Nuclear AARS1 binds to the promoters of oncogenes (e.g., YAP, c-MYC) and tumor suppressors (e.g., p53), modulating their expression. For example, in gastric cancer, nuclear AARS1 lactylates YAP, promoting its nuclear retention and transcriptional activity—driving cell proliferation and invasion [18].

sec.title: DNA damage repair
sec.p: AARS1 interacts with DNA repair proteins (e.g., MRE11, BRCA1) in the nucleus, enhancing homologous recombination (HR) repair. This reduces the efficacy of DNA-damaging agents (e.g., cisplatin), contributing to chemoresistance [6, 19].

Notably, nuclear AARS1 levels correlate with tumor grade: in high-grade lung adenocarcinomas, 65% of cells show nuclear AARS1 localization, compared to only 12% in low-grade tumors [5]. This suggests that AARS1 nuclear translocation is a late event in malignant progression.

sec.title: AARS1-mediated lysine lactylation: a link between metabolism and oncogenesis
sec.p: The Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis) in tumors leads to excessive lactate accumulation (10–20 mM in the tumor microenvironment, vs. 1–2 mM in normal tissues) [4, 5]. AARS1 senses this lactate and catalyzes lysine lactylation—a PTM that regulates protein function by altering charge, structure, or protein-protein interactions [4–6]. Beyond its prominent role in cancer, lysine lactylation has also been observed in non-malignant contexts, including histone modifications mediated by HDAC1, underscoring its widespread biological relevance [20].

sec.title: Mechanism of AARS1-mediated lactylation
sec.p: AARS1’s ability to switch between canonical aminoacylation and non-canonical lactylation is a remarkable example of metabolic plasticity. This shift is mechanistically linked to its aminoacylation domain, which possesses a binding site capable of accommodating both alanine and lactate. The reaction proceeds via two ATP-dependent steps, analogous to its canonical function (Fig. 3):

list-item.p: Lactate Activation and Competitive Binding: In the presence of ATP, AARS1 can bind either alanine or lactate. When lactate levels are low, AARS1 primarily binds alanine, forming alanyl-AMP, which is then transferred to tRNA^Ala for protein synthesis. However, under conditions of high lactate concentration, such as those found in the tumor microenvironment, lactate competes effectively with alanine for binding within the aminoacylation domain [5, 6]. This competitive binding event is crucial: high lactate levels shift the equilibrium towards the formation of a lactate-AMP intermediate. Recent studies have elucidated that high lactate concentrations can induce conformational changes in AARS1, favoring the activation of lactate over alanine, thereby reprogramming AARS1’s enzymatic preference from aminoacylation to lactylation (Li et al., 2024). This metabolic sensing and functional switch is a pivotal mechanism by which AARS1 bridges altered tumor metabolism with downstream signaling.

Lactate Transfer: The lactyl moiety from lactate-AMP is covalently attached to the ε-amino group of lysine residues in substrate proteins, generating lactylated proteins and releasing AMP [5, 19]. The precise concentration thresholds and kinetic parameters governing the switch between aminoacylation and lactylation are key areas of ongoing research, but the competition for binding within the aminoacylation domain, influenced by local lactate levels, is understood to be the primary driver of this metabolic plasticity.

caption.p: The two-step lactylation reaction catalyzed by AARS1. This figure illustrates the biochemical mechanism by which AARS1 functions as a lactyltransferase

sec.p: Step 1: Lactate Activation and Formation of Lactate-AMP Intermediate. Under conditions of high lactate concentration, characteristic of the tumor microenvironment, lactate competes with alanine for binding within the aminoacylation domain of AARS1. In the presence of ATP, AARS1 catalyzes the activation of lactate, forming a high-energy lactate-AMP intermediate, analogous to the alanyl-AMP intermediate formed during canonical aminoacylation. This activation step involves the transfer of the adenylate moiety from ATP to lactate, with the concomitant release of pyrophosphate (PPi). The ability of AARS1’s active site to accommodate lactate and utilize ATP for its activation is a key aspect of its metabolic sensing capability.

Step 2: Lactate Transfer to Substrate Proteins. The activated lactyl group from the lactate-AMP intermediate is then covalently transferred to the ε-amino group of specific lysine residues on substrate proteins, resulting in the formation of lactylated proteins and the release of AMP.

Proteomic studies have identified > 500 lactylation substrates of AARS1 in tumor cells, including transcription factors (p53, YAP), metabolic enzymes (PKM2, LDHA), and DNA repair proteins (MRE11) [5, 6, 18, 19]. These substrates are involved in cell cycle regulation, metabolism, and stress response—key pathways for tumor survival. It is important to acknowledge that proteomic studies, while powerful for initial identification, can sometimes yield false positives. Therefore, rigorous validation of high-confidence lactylation targets using orthogonal assays, such as in vitro lactylation assays with purified recombinant AARS1 and specific peptides or proteins, is crucial. Recent studies have employed such validation strategies for key substrates like lactylations [21], providing stronger evidence for AARS1’s role in modifying these proteins.

sec.title: Lactylation of p53: a canonical oncogenic mechanism
sec.p: The tumor suppressor p53 is a major AARS1 lactylation substrate. In normal cells, p53 is activated by DNA damage, inducing expression of downstream target genes (e.g., p21, Bax) that trigger cell cycle arrest or apoptosis [5, 6]. In tumors, AARS1 lactylates p53 at two key residues in its DNA-binding domain: K120 and K139 (Fig. 4): (1) Disrupted DNA Binding: Lactylation of K120 (a residue critical for p53-DNA interaction) reduces p53’s affinity for target gene promoters by 4–5-fold [5] (2). Impaired Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation (LLPS): p53 forms nuclear condensates via LLPS to enhance its transcriptional activity. Lactylation of K139 disrupts these condensates, further inhibiting p53 function [5]. In patients with wild-type p53 (≈ 50% of human cancers), AARS1 expression and p53 lactylation levels are inversely correlated with overall survival. For example, in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with wild-type p53, high AARS1/p53 lactylation is associated with a 2.8-fold higher risk of death compared to low levels [5]. This highlights AARS1-mediated p53 lactylation as a critical mechanism of tumor suppressor inactivation in cancer.

caption.p: AARS1-mediated p53 lactylation inhibits its tumor suppressor function. Lactylation at K120 disrupts p53-DNA binding, while lactylation at K139 impairs LLPS. Both effects reduce p53 transcriptional activity, preventing expression of downstream tumor suppressor genes (e.g., p21, Bax) and promoting tumor cell survival

sec.title: Lactylation of metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins
sec.p: Beyond transcription factors like p53 and YAP, AARS1-mediated lactylation targets a diverse array of proteins involved in critical cellular processes, including metabolism and DNA damage repair. This broad substrate specificity underscores the pervasive influence of lactylation in cancer biology.

For example, PKM2 (Pyruvate Kinase M2), a key glycolytic enzyme that plays a central role in the Warburg effect, has been identified as a lactylation substrate. Lactylation of PKM2 can modulate its enzymatic activity and its role in promoting tumor cell proliferation and survival. While the precise functional consequences of PKM2 lactylation are still being elucidated, it suggests that lactylation may directly impact metabolic flux and tumor energetics.

Furthermore, MRE11, a component of the MRN complex essential for DNA double-strand break repair, is another significant lactylation substrate. AARS1-mediated lactylation of MRE11 has been shown to enhance its recruitment to DNA damage sites and promote homologous recombination repair [19, 22]. This enhances the DNA repair capacity of cancer cells, contributing to resistance against genotoxic chemotherapy.

These examples, spanning metabolic enzymes and DNA repair proteins, highlight that AARS1-mediated lactylation extends far beyond transcriptional regulation, impacting fundamental cellular processes that are critical for tumor initiation, progression, and treatment resistance. This broad spectrum of substrates provides a more holistic view of lactylation’s role in cancer, demonstrating its capacity to fine-tune diverse cellular pathways.

sec.title: Interplay with other metabolic post-translational modifications (PTMs)
sec.p: While the focus has been on lactylation, it is crucial to consider how this modification might intersect with other prevalent metabolic PTMs, such as acetylation and succinylation. These modifications, also occurring on lysine residues, can influence protein function by altering charge and interaction networks. It is plausible that lactylation may compete with acetylation or succinylation for binding to the same lysine residues on certain substrates, thereby modulating the functional outcome of these competing modifications. Alternatively, lactylation could act in concert with or antagonize other PTMs, creating complex regulatory layers that govern protein activity and cellular fate [23, 24]. However, the precise mechanisms by which AARS1-mediated lactylation cross-talks with other metabolic PTMs remain an exciting area for future investigation.

sec.title: AARS1 mutations in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT)
sec.p: CMT disease is the most common inherited peripheral neuropathy (prevalence: 1 in 2500), with CMT2N (a subtype caused by AARS1 mutations) accounting for 2–5% of cases [7–9]. AARS1 mutations in CMT2N are diverse, affecting all three domains—but their pathogenicity is not driven by loss of aminoacylation activity (unlike canonical AARS1 dysfunction). Instead, two key mechanisms have been identified:

sec.title: Aberrant interaction with neuropilin 1 (NRP1)
sec.p: NRP1 is a transmembrane receptor that mediates neurotrophic signaling (via binding to vascular endothelial growth factor A, VEGF-A). All CMT2N-associated AARS1 mutations (e.g., R329H, N71Y, E788A) enhance AARS1-NRP1 binding—displacing VEGF-A and blocking neurotrophic signaling [9, 15, 25]. Recent structural studies have provided key insights into the interaction between AARS1 and NRP1, revealing how specific mutations disrupt the normal functional interplay and lead to aberrant signaling cascades [5]. This leads to axonal degeneration, demyelination, and progressive motor and sensory dysfunction (e.g., muscle weakness, numbness in extremities). For example, the R329H mutation—identified in 8 CMT families across 4 countries—does not alter AARS1’s aminoacylation activity but increases its affinity for NRP1 by 3-fold, leading to severe axonal loss in peripheral nerves [9, 15].

sec.title: Disrupted axonal transport
sec.p: AARS1 mutations (e.g., G102R in the aminoacylation domain) impair its interaction with microtubule-associated proteins (e.g., tau), disrupting axonal transport of tRNAs and proteins. This leads to reduced protein synthesis in axon terminals, contributing to neuronal degeneration [8, 26].

Clinical phenotypes of CMT2N vary by mutation but typically include early-onset (childhood/adolescence) progressive weakness, reduced reflexes, and electrophysiological evidence of axonal neuropathy (e.g., reduced motor nerve conduction velocity < 45 m/s) [7, 25]. Notably, some patients with the R329H mutation present with reversible white matter lesions, which may mimic stroke or encephalitis—highlighting the need for genetic testing to avoid misdiagnosis [15].

sec.title: AARS1 in neurodegenerative and white matter diseases
sec.p: Beyond CMT2N, AARS1 mutations drive other neurological disorders by disrupting protein homeostasis and ER stress responses:

sec.title: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP)
sec.p: ALSP is a rare neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, dysarthria, and white matter lesions. A homozygous non-synonymous mutation (AARS1: NM_001605:exon14:c.1817 C > T:p.Thr606Ile) in the editing domain of AARS1 was identified as a causative factor in a Chinese family with ALSP [12]. This mutation impairs AARS1’s proofreading activity, leading to accumulation of mischarged Ser-tRNA^Ala and misfolded proteins. The resulting ER stress activates the PERK-eIF2α pathway, triggering neuronal apoptosis and white matter degeneration [12, 17]. Clinical manifestations in affected individuals included progressive blurred vision, hypertonia, and severe emaciation (BMI 13.36)—consistent with widespread neuronal loss [12].

sec.title: Zebrafish models of neurodegeneration
sec.p: Zebrafish with a homozygous ars1^cq71/cq71 mutation (orthologous to human AARS1) exhibit defects in neural progenitor cell (NPC) maintenance. The mutation activates the ER stress-induced PERK signaling pathway, which upregulates nfe2l2b (encoding Nrf2). Nrf2 then binds to the p53 promoter, driving p53-mediated NPC apoptosis [27]. This leads to reduced neurogenesis and progressive neurodegeneration—mimicking human AARS1-related white matter disease. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of PERK reversed NPC loss in zebrafish, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for human disorders [27].

sec.title: AARS1 in metabolic and rare diseases
sec.p: AARS1 dysfunction also contributes to non-neurological disorders, primarily via impaired protein synthesis and metabolic dysregulation:

sec.title: Recurrent acute liver failure
sec.p: The first case of AARS1-related liver disease was reported in a child with two missense mutations (p.Leu298Gln and p.Arg751Gly) in the aminoacylation domain [8]. These mutations reduced AARS1 protein stability (by 40%) and enzymatic activity (by 60%) in fibroblasts, leading to impaired protein synthesis in hepatocytes. Clinical manifestations included recurrent acute liver failure (ALT/AST > 1000 U/L), coagulopathy, and hyperammonemia—requiring liver transplantation at age 5 [10]. This case highlights AARS1’s critical role in maintaining liver function, likely via supporting the high protein synthesis demands of hepatocytes.

sec.title: Sulfide dysplasia
sec.p: Sulfide dysplasia is a rare disorder characterized by abnormal sulfur metabolism and connective tissue defects. AARS1 mutations (e.g., p.Arg751Gly) reduce its ability to interact with cysteine synthase—an enzyme involved in cysteine (a precursor of sulfur-containing molecules) synthesis. This leads to reduced cysteine levels, impaired sulfide metabolism, and connective tissue abnormalities (e.g., joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility) [13]. While the mechanism is not fully elucidated, it suggests a novel non-canonical role of AARS1 in metabolic pathway crosstalk.

sec.title: Unresolved mechanisms: from structure to substrates
sec.p: Despite recent advances, key questions about AARS1’s biology remain unanswered:

sec.title: Structural basis of lactate sensing
sec.p: While AARS1 is known to bind lactate, the atomic structure of the AARS1-lactate complex has not been resolved. This structural information is critical for understanding how lactate binding induces conformational changes that allosterically switch AARS1 from its canonical aminoacylation role to its non-canonical lactyltransferase activity. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) studies of AARS1 in complex with lactate, ATP, and potential protein substrates could reveal detailed atomic interactions. Such structural insights will be pivotal for the rational design of highly specific inhibitors targeting its lactyltransferase function [5, 6]. In fact, recent advances in frozen EM have provided high-resolution structures for other aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, such as leurs, to form complexes with their homologous tRNAs and ligands, such as leurs ligand structures. These studies demonstrate the ability of cryo em in elucidating ligand induced conformational dynamics and substrate recognition mechanisms in AARS family. Applying a similar frozen EM method to aars1 can obtain valuable insights about its lactic acid binding capsule and the subsequent allosteric transformation controlling its dual enzyme activity [28].

sec.title: Full spectrum of lactylation substrates
sec.p: To date, only ~ 500 AARS1 lactylation substrates have been identified (via proteomics in cancer cells) [5, 18]. However, the full spectrum distribution of AARS1 lactylated substrate under different physiological and pathological conditions, including non cancerous tissues, remains to be further studied. Systematic screening in these different cellular environments is essential for revealing tissue-specific substrates. Identification of these substrates will clarify the effects of aars1 mediated lactylation in various cellular processes and disease mechanisms.

sec.title: Tissue-specific regulation of AARS1
sec.p: AARS1’s function varies by cell type (e.g., lactylation in tumors vs. translation in normal cells), but the regulatory mechanisms (e.g., post-translational modifications, cofactors) driving this specificity are unknown. Emerging technologies such as single cell RNA sequencing and spatial proteomics provide powerful tools for mapping AARS1 expression, localization and interaction groups in a cell type specific manner. Understanding these regulatory networks is essential to analyze the role of aars1 and formulate targeted treatment interventions.

sec.title: Therapeutic development: targeting AARS1 in disease
sec.p: AARS1 represents a promising therapeutic target, but several challenges must be addressed to translate basic research into clinical applications:

sec.title: Lactyltransferase inhibitors
sec.p: Compounds that block AARS1’s lactate-AMP formation step (e.g., competitive inhibitors of the aminoacylation domain) could reduce p53 lactylation and restore its tumor suppressor function. A recent study identified a small molecule (LAC-1) that binds to AARS1’s lactate-binding pocket, inhibiting lactylation of p53 and YAP in gastric cancer cells—reducing tumor growth in mouse xenografts by 60% [18]. Further optimization of LAC-1’s potency and selectivity (to avoid off-target effects on canonical AARS1 activity) is ongoing. This approach holds significant potential for restoring tumor suppressor function and inhibiting cancer progression.

sec.title: Nuclear import inhibitors
sec.p: Peptides that block AARS1’s nuclear localization signal (NLS) could prevent its nuclear translocation, inhibiting transcriptional regulation of oncogenes. Preclinical studies in lung cancer models showed that NLS-blocking peptides reduced nuclear AARS1 levels by 70% and sensitized tumors to cisplatin [5]. This strategy offers a way to disrupt AARS1’s oncogenic nuclear functions and enhance chemosensitivity, representing a crucial translational step in cancer treatment.

sec.title: CMT2N
sec.p: Monoclonal antibodies targeting the AARS1-NRP1 interaction could restore VEGF-A signaling. In vitro studies showed that anti-NRP1 antibodies displaced AARS1 from NRP1, increasing VEGF-A binding by 4-fold and promoting neurite outgrowth [9]. Clinical trials of such antibodies in CMT patients are pending, representing a key translational effort to address the root cause of neurodegeneration in CMT2N.

sec.title: Neurodegeneration
sec.p: PERK inhibitors (e.g., GSK2606414) could reverse ER stress-induced neuronal apoptosis in ALSP and zebrafish models. In zebrafish with ars1 mutations, GSK2606414 reduced NPC apoptosis by 50% and restored neurogenesis [27]. Repurposing PERK inhibitors (already in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease) for AARS1-related neurodegeneration could accelerate translation. Repurposing PERK inhibitors (already in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease) for AARS1-related neurodegeneration could accelerate translation, offering a promising therapeutic avenue for these rare disorders.

sec.title: Diagnostic and prognostic applications of AARS1
sec.p: AARS1 has significant potential as a biomarker for disease diagnosis and prognosis:

sec.title: Cancer
sec.p: Detection of AARS1 expression (via IHC) or p53 lactylation (via mass spectrometry) in tumor biopsies could stratify patients for treatment. For example, high AARS1/p53 lactylation in NSCLC patients with wild-type p53 predicts poor response to chemotherapy—identifying candidates for AARS1 inhibitor combination therapy [5]. This offers a direct translational application for patient stratification and personalized treatment strategies.

sec.title: CMT2N
sec.p: Genetic testing for AARS1 mutations (e.g., R329H) could improve diagnosis in patients with axonal neuropathy and reversible white matter lesions, avoiding misdiagnosis as stroke or encephalitis [15]. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for timely management and genetic counseling.

sec.title: Liver failure
sec.p: Measurement of AARS1 protein levels in liver biopsies or serum could identify patients at risk of recurrent acute liver failure, enabling early intervention (e.g., liver transplantation) [10]. This provides a potential diagnostic tool for early risk assessment and proactive management.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Alanyl-tRNA Synthetase 1 (AARS1) has emerged as a multifunctional protein with critical roles in protein synthesis, metabolic sensing, and disease pathogenesis. Its ability to sense lactate and catalyze lysine lactylation links the Warburg effect to tumor progression—offering a novel mechanism for targeting cancer metabolism. In non-malignant disorders, AARS1 mutations drive neuropathy (CMT2N), neurodegeneration (ALSP), and liver failure via distinct mechanisms (e.g., NRP1 dysregulation, ER stress).

While significant progress has been made, key challenges remain: resolving the structural basis of AARS1’s lactyltransferase activity, identifying tissue-specific lactylation substrates, and developing selective therapeutics that avoid disrupting canonical protein synthesis. Addressing these gaps will not only deepen our understanding of AARS1’s biology but also unlock its potential as a therapeutic target and biomarker for a spectrum of diseases—from cancer to rare neurological disorders.

Future research should integrate structural biology (e.g., cryo-EM of AARS1-lactate complexes), single-cell omics (to map AARS1’s cell-type-specific functions), and clinical trials (to test AARS1 inhibitors in cancer and CMT2N). By bridging basic and translational research, AARS1 could become a cornerstone of precision medicine for diverse disorders.
